related_work: This week I used Seth Giddings’ reading Why Look at Toys? It helped me understand that toys can be open, flexible and playful. I also looked at Amsterdam Real Time, where people’s daily routes became a map. Ge Yu Road showed me that a map can make a fictional place feel real. These works helped me think about play, maps and power.
conclusion_future_work: My answer is that toys and maps can shape how people feel and act. In my future work, I want to make an interactive installation for children in hospital waiting areas. I hope it can feel playful and safe, helping children explore, relax and feel less worried while they wait.
results_discussion:
After reading and watching the lecture examples, I understood that toys and maps are not as simple as they first appear. Toys can give people freedom to touch, test and imagine. They do not always need one correct use. Maps also look simple, but they can influence what people believe about a place. For example, Ge Yu Road showed that a name on a map can make something fictional feel real. Amsterdam Real Time also showed that a map can record people’s daily movement and time, not only streets and buildings.
The most surprising idea for me was that maps can have power. They may look objective, but someone chooses what to include, what to name and what to hide. This made me think that interactive work can also guide people’s attention.
title: week 4 in ideas
introduction:
The two lectures made me think about how everyday objects and systems can shape the way we understand the world. In the lecture about toys and games, I learned that toys are not only for children. They can also be small experiments or models for new ideas. A toy is often open and flexible. People can touch it, move it and use it in their own way. This is different from a game, because a game usually has clear rules, goals and winners. I think this is important for my own practice because I want to make work that does not control people too much. I want users to have space to explore, imagine and create their own meaning.
The digital mapping lecture connected with this idea in a surprising way. Before, I thought a map simply showed the real world. However, the lecture showed that maps are not neutral. They choose names, borders, routes and points of view, so they can also show power. For example, Ge Yu Road started as a fake street sign, but after it appeared in official systems and maps, it slowly became real to many people. This made me realise that digital systems can change reality, not only record it. Both lectures made me think about openness. A toy can invite people to use it in unexpected ways, and a map can be changed to show personal memories, feelings or hidden stories. In my future work, I would like to make an interactive object that feels simple and playful, but also makes people question what they usually accept as normal or true.
